Welcome back to Altium Academy.
I'm your host, Zach Peterson.

Today, we're gonna be
answering a viewer question

about our classic "One
Minute Design Review" series.

Now, unless you've been
living under a rock

or you're just not
subscribed to the channel,
then you probably know

about the "One Minute
Design Review" series.

Tons of designers have been
sending us so many great designs
and we got a great viewer question
about these design reviews,

and what really makes a great
design review submission.

Let's go ahead and check
out that viewer question

and get started.
(upbeat music)
Now, the "One Minute Design Review" series
contains reviews of PCB designs

that have been sent in from
designers all over the world,

to be able to review these

and show them on the
Altium Academy channel.
We've seen some really great stuff,
a ton of ESP32 designs,

learning experience for me

a really great question

This question comes from the
recent design review we filmed

for Joshua Anthony's 60-volt

that make a truly excellent
design review submission?

I recall data sheets,
BOM, clearing DRC errors,
why are these so prevalent,

Justin, this is an excellent question,
and no, that video doesn't exist,

which is why we're here
filming it right now.

What I wanna do now is run
over some of the designs
that we've reviewed on the channel,
and we reviewed over 100 at this point.

So unfortunately I can't
go through them all.

that exhibit some of
the common good things

So let's hop into Altium and take a look.
So first, let's take a look at this design

Now, first things first,

the cover page, and then
we get into some circuitry
by the third page.
You can see how good the organization is

Now, as I scroll through here,

eventually we get to a
power sequencing page.
This is another thing

which of course doesn't
get used in the PCB layout,

piece of documentation

electrical documentation
for the device.
So here we have power sequencing,

of this type of documentation
inside schematics
in other projects.

but this is something

that you will see in
project documentation.

And of course, because
schematics are the root source

for a given revision, it
is important to include
that revision history somewhere,

The last thing that we

Good job on this.

who was involved in the design,

the company that has the

et cetera, et cetera.

A lot of times we see schematics

that just have the basic
default title block from Altium,

the default Altium templates

You're free to do that, but
I always encourage people
to develop their own title block.

Whether you're doing
it in the PCB doc file

So make sure to go out

Next, let's take a look
at another example.
This example comes from Saviour Emmanuel,

organization in the schematics.

So here on page one, we

that can be pretty tough.

flat set of schematics

And one thing I like
about this block diagram

right here the signals

that are going between the
different blocks in this system.

As we click through some of
these other schematic sheets,
you can see here that there's also

a power tree diagram in
page two, I like that.

You need to have a power
tree diagram somewhere

for your documentation
or your specification,

makes sense to include
it in your schematics,
and that also helps someone like me
when I'm doing a design review.
When we go to the other sheets,
you can see here again,
we have really great organization.

We have a sheet
specifically for the STM32,

it's reset pin, and then
a couple of connectors

that you would use for
debug and programming.
Going through here,
you can see we have our Ethernet page.
It makes sense to put the connector
for the Ethernet PHY in the same sheet
as the Ethernet PHY.

You can see we've done
that here on this page.
Here in the motor driver,

you can also see we've done
essentially the same thing.

The connector for the motor
driver is in the same page
as the motor driver circuit,
and so on and so forth as we click through
some of these other pages.
Now, everything I just mentioned deals
with the organization of the schematics,
which is really important

if you're going to have your
design reviewed by a peer.

But what about the actual
contents of your CAD models
and your schematic symbols?
Let's take a look here in this same design
from Saviour Emmanuel.
Now, here as we click through

some of these components
in this schematic sheet,

you can see here that we have
a few important parameters

that I point out in a lot of
design review submissions.

One of these parameters is
the manufacturer part number,
and then another one is the manufacturer.
Now, it's really important
to include that information somewhere
for all of your parts.
And the reason should be obvious.

You wanna make sure that if
you're doing a BOM export
from your Altium schematics
that you pull the manufacturer name

and the manufacturer part
number into that BOM.
And the fastest way to do that
is to set up an out-job file,

and have the out-job file
point to those two parameters

for inclusion as one of
the columns in your BOM.

Now, you don't have to
literally name this parameter,
"Manufacturer Part Number."
You could name it "MFG Part Number",
"MFGPN", "Manufacturer PN".
We've seen all sorts of variations,
and really any of them is acceptable
as long as you're consistent.

Make sure that if you use
manufacturer part number
on one of these components,
you can see here it's used
on all of these other components

that I've clicked on
so far in this design.

So make sure you enforce that
same level of consistency
that you would enforce in your title block
and all of your other documentation
in your schematic symbols.

Now, as I click through
some of these components

and I look through some
of these other sheets,

you can see here that
in the Properties panel,
there are some other parameters

listed in each of the parts
that are certainly useful

but aren't mandatory for
sourcing your components.
Manufacturer and manufacturer part number
are good enough to go into pretty much
any procurement system,

upload your BOM, and very
quickly create orders.

You can also do the same
thing from Octopart.
If you go to Octopart.com,
and click on the BOM tool link,
you'll be able to upload your BOM export
from your Altium project.

And from there, you can create
carts on distributor website
where you can then make parts purchases.

Some of these other
parameters that are helpful
are the case and the package.
Of course, it's very nice to know
that this CH340C component isn't SOIC16.
And then you can see here,
we have some supplier information.
So for example, we have a desired supplier
that we've chosen here, it's LCSC,
and then we have a supplier part number,
and then we have an alternate part number
listed here as a parameter.

But of course, there isn't
one chosen at this time.
So all of this is very good
for creating your schematic symbols,
and I think that's one of the things

that makes a great
design review submission.
Now, let's jump over

to this other schematic
from Teguh Nugraha,
and we can see a few other things

that I think make a great
design review submission.

Here, we only have one
schematic sheet in this project,

but if we scroll in
and we just take a look

at some of the characteristics
on this schematic,

you'll see a few things that
make a great submission.
So here we see, again,
consistency in our net naming format.
As you can see here,

for everything along this
gigabit Ethernet connector.

Here, you can also see
for these resistors,
we're actually showing the value
of the resistor in a comment, very good.

So that comment is
visible in the schematic.

And then here, you can
see that this comment
is keyed to a value that is specified

as one of the parameters
here in the Properties panel.
Same thing with these capacitors.
The value of the capacitor is visible.

I don't want to have to then
click on this capacitor,
grab the part number, put them to Google,

and look up what the value
of that capacitor is.

Next on these differential
pairs for our USB interface,

we've used the differential
pair directive,

very good, because they
do need to be routed
as differential pairs.

And in order to use the
differential routing tools
in the PCB editor, you have to assign

the differential pair
directive to these nets.
Another thing that I like here

is that we've used nets
that very closely match
the pin name on some of these components,
which makes a lot of sense too.

And using nets that match
the pin name is very nice
because sometimes in the PCB layout,
you will see a net name,
and it's not always clear
exactly what the function of that net is.
But hey, assigning these names to nets,
even if the only place they go to

is just one of these
pins on this component,
is very helpful for understanding
what that trace is doing

or what that signal on
that trace is doing,

and where it is connected
to in the design.
Finally, a really good practice
on all of these integrated circuits
is to include the part number
for the integrated circuit as a comment,
and not just a generic part number
or a part number family,
but the actual part number

that you would put in to
order this specific component.

So that's been done on all
of these components here,

as you can see as I
look through the design.
So that's a brief summary
of what I like to see in schematics

and some of our better
design review submissions.
And everything I've mentioned there
is really what you would expect to see
in a professional project.
I always try to implement those guidelines
that I've just given you in the schematics

whenever I deliver a
finalized project to a client,

and I would expect that
all the designers out there
should do the same.
Now, let's take a look at some examples
of what makes a great PCB layout
and some examples of some things
that you shouldn't do in your designs.

Here I have a PCB layout pulled
up from Jakhanggwra Narzary.
This PCB layout is a 10-layer PCB
with multiple internal planes.
You can see here that all of the planes
are very clearly named,
and the names are accurate

in terms of how they
represent the function
of each of those layers.

So we have signal layers
very clearly labeled,

we have ground layers
very clearly labeled,

and then we have our top
and bottom component layers.
Now, a lot of times, the basic layout
that we see in these designs is very good.

Sometimes you could consolidate
things onto one layer,
sometimes it's gonna make more sense
to put things onto two layers,

and I try to mention that
in these design reviews.
But of course, it's never mandatory
to do every layout a specific way.
There are multiple factors
and constraints you have to consider,
and I really leave it up to the designers
to figure that out.

One of the big things I often
look for is the silkscreen,
that comes up very often.
Another thing that I often look for

is did you design all
of these copper features

in accordance with
manufacturer capabilities?

So this is a pretty good
design review example
that shows success in both areas.

So here, if we just zoom
in on some of these traces,

you can see here, for example,
if I select this trace,
this is a 4.6 mil wide trace.
Every manufacturer on the planet

is gonna have no problem
producing a design
with a 4.6 mil wide trace.

Here you can see that the
spacing is also consistent
with what you would find
with most manufacturer capabilities.
If we click on the via,
you can see here this via only goes down
to about eight mil drill diameter,

and then the pad diameter
is properly oversized

for this drill in order to
account for drill wander.
So those are all good things.
It illustrates a basic understanding
of both the manufacturing process
as well as the manufacturing capabilities
of most PCB manufacturers
under a standard subtractive etch process.

Now, of course, some of
these lines are a bit thin.
You have these two lines here
that are part of a differential pair,
and you can see here that these lines

are 2.926 mils wide, so
they are a little thin.
Some manufacturers may quote you
at a more expensive fabrication cost
due to the more advanced etching process,

but of course, sometimes that
is necessary in your design.
So you have to determine as the engineer

whether or not that is
going to be necessary
for your specific design.
I would argue in this design,
it may not be necessary,

you could probably space
those traces out a little bit
just to increase the width.

There's no need to make
those traces super thin
if you don't have to make them super thin.
Now, just zooming out and scanning

around a little bit on
some of these components,
what I see here on these passives

is a lot of consistency,
which is really great.
It's nice to see that these footprints

have all basically been
created by the same person
because I see similar design standards

being implemented in
all of these footprints.
Here you can see we have an outline
for these components.

We can see that we have
similar type of pad shapes,
we have rounded edges on these pads.
And then you can see here
that we have similar silkscreen size

for all the reference
designators everywhere.

Now, even though there is
consistency in the footprints,

there are still some
mistakes in this board.

One of the big ones that
we have talked about
in some of our footprints videos,
and I've talked about on my channel
in terms of footprints,
I've also talked about this

with Elizabeth Bustamante
on a podcast episode,
is of course, the embedding of vias
directly into PCB footprints.
In my opinion, this is a big no-no,
you should absolutely not do this.
And even though some of the parts
in the manufacturer parts search panel

do come into Altium with vias
embedded into the footprint,
you should still edit those out
because in some cases,
you might wanna remove some of these vias
to open up some more room
for routing on the inner layers.
So it's a good idea to keep these vias

out of these die-attached
pads on these footprints.
Next, I want to go into 3D
and take a look at the silkscreen,

because this is one of
the more common things
that comes up very often.
Here, as I scroll around in 3D,
we can see that most of the silkscreen
is done very well on this board,
but we do see some footprints
that need some fixes to the silkscreen.
You can see right here on U14,

we have silkscreen overlapping
with exposed copper pads.
When I zoom out and go over here

to switch one and switch
two, we have the same thing.
We have the switch outline

falling right onto the
exposed pads and holes
for this footprint.

Now, sometimes the silkscreen
doesn't fall directly
onto an exposed copper pad,
but it does fall pretty close
to the solder mask opening,

as you can see here in the
footprint for this test point.

And we even have a little
bit of a leftover line here

that we should delete in the
library for this component.
Now, all of these points I mentioned

about silkscreen embedded
into the component
falling onto exposed copper
can be fixed using an automated tool.

Now, of course, I can select
one of these components.
I can unlock the primitives here,
and this is going to allow me
to manually edit these silkscreen lines
directly inside the PCB layout.
But one tool that you can use
that will automate all this
is the Silkscreen Preparation tool
from inside the Tools menu.

Inside the Silkscreen
Preparation dialogue,

you can have the tool
apply to all footprints
or only your selected footprints,

and it will basically clear
out any of that silkscreen
that's falling onto exposed copper.

Now, if you have an issue
like you see here with TP2
where the silkscreen is getting too close
to the solder mask opening,
you do wanna check to see

that the solder mask
opening is not too large,
and that happens inside the design rules.
And I'll get into the design rules more
here in just a moment.

The last thing I wanna
mention with the silkscreen
is the placement of reference designators.
And I actually go through and clean up
all of the reference designator placements

at the very end of the
design using the 3D view.

So inside the 3D view,
with the Selection Filter,
you can select texts only,
and when you do that, be able to pick up
any of these reference designators in 3D,

and move them around like
I'm showing here on screen.
I prefer to do this in 3D
rather than going into the 2D view
and turning on just the paste mask opening
and just the silkscreen layer
and trying to do it that way,
because when you see it in 3D,
you know it's gonna be accurate
and appear this way in the board
once it's actually fabricated.

Let's take a look here
at Teguh Nugraha's board,
and we can see some other things
that I like to see in designs.
Now, here we do have a net antenna error
that needs to be resolved,

so he's gonna have to go
back into the original design
in order to fix that.
But one thing that I do like to see
in some of these designs
is that you actually used the Altium tools

in order to put some of
these more advanced features
into the PCB.
So one great example here
is the length tuning segments.
You can see here that

with the other options selected
in the selection filter,
if I just select this region of the board
with the length tuning section,
this length tuning is actually placed

as a length tuning object
in Altium Designer.
Now, you are free to draw in

these length tuning sections
as arcs if you want to,

and I do sometimes do that
when the arcs are very small,
maybe I only need one of those arcs

of two different nets in the design.
Another great example
of using the built-in objects
in Altium Designer is teardrops.
You can see here on some of these pads,
we do have teardrops applied.

I would advise that you
apply them consistently.
You can see here

that they haven't been
applied consistently.

There is a polygon region
that has been auto-created
and appears on this trace.

This gets auto-created
using the teardrop tool
from the Tools menu.
Now, if you thought drawing in
length tuning sections by hand was a pain,
try drawing in teardrop sections by hand
nobody wants to do that.
So these appear in an automated way,
and you can see here that we would prefer

to do this using the
automated tools in Altium
rather than drawing them out by hand.
Now, there's one last thing
that Justin Shaedo mentioned

in his question on that
design review video,
and that was design rule violations.
Sometimes we see dozens or even hundreds

of leftover design rule
violations in these boards

that get submitted for a
"One Minute Design Review".

Now, a lot of times
there are real violations

that need to be addressed
in that list of DRC errors.
However, quite a few of those DRC errors
can be fixed just by changing

the default design rules
to more realistic values.

So what I have here on
screen is a blank PCB,

and if you go into the
Design and Rules option
in this blank PCB, you will see

that we have a bunch of
design rules of course,

but they're all filled
in with default values.
Now, these default values
aren't chosen for any particular reason

other than the fact that
we have to have something
in all of these.

So the developers decided to
fill in these numbers, right?

You can't fault 'em for
filling in something,
because no matter what they choose,
it's probably gonna be wrong.
But it's your job as the design engineer
to go through this list of design rules
and fill in the appropriate values
that match your fabricator's capabilities
for building this PCB.

Now, clearances and routing
widths are kind of common.
We've seen them in multiple design reviews
needing to be changed,

but I think one of the
most common design rules
that needs to be edited
in order to make a really great design
is the Board Outline Clearance.
Sometimes this rule is not used at all,
and designers will draw a keep out
around the edge of the board

in order to enforce a
clearance from the board edge.

Now, there is a built-in board
clearance rule to enable it.
Just right click, hit New Rule,

as you just saw me do, and
then you can go in here,

and then you can set board
clearances to the edge
for all objects in the design.
So what I normally do is I set a 10 mil
or .25 millimeter clearance by default
in all new PCBs that I build.
That's going to ensure that any copper

that would extend up to
the edge of the board,
such as any planes you have in the design,
have enough clearance to the board edge
so that when the board is depanelized,

there is no copper exposed
through the edge of the PCB.

Another very common one
is solder mask expansion.

I often see the solder
mask expansion value
is left at four mils wide.
And in simple SMD components
or through-hole components

that have a lot of
spacing between the pins,
four mils is just fine.

But if you look at a lot
of integrated circuits
such as that have a QFN or a QFP package,
that four-mil expansion is much too large

because it will leave two
small of a solder masks sliver

between those two neighboring
pads in the package.
The other thing that can happen

is it will fully open the
solder mask around those pads,
and when you fully open the solder mask
on two neighboring pads,
you create a high risk
of a short circuit during soldering.

Now, I've said in many
of these design reviews,

a good value to use for
the solder mask expansion

in pretty much every design
I've worked with is one mil.
Why one mil?
Well, that leaves a little bit of error

for misregistration when
the board is laminated
and your stackup is built.

That also ensures that
you don't leave too small
of a solder mask between pads

on some of those finer pitch
packages like QFNs or QFPs.

Now, these aren't the
only default design rules

that you might need to
change in your design.

Go back and watch some
of those design reviews

and you'll be able to
see some other examples
of default design rules that should change
in order to prevent DRC errors
that aren't actually a problem
when you go to build your board.

Thank you, Justin Shaedo,
for the great question,
and thank you all the designers out there

for sending in these
design review submissions.

And don't stop, if you
have something great
that you wanna show off on the channel,

find me on LinkedIn, send
me your design files,
or send me your manufacturing files,
and we'll create a review of your design.

Thanks to everybody for
watching this video.
Make sure to hit that Like button,
hit the Subscribe button,

leave your comments and questions
in the comments section.
And of course,

don't forget to call
your fabricator, folks.
We'll see you next time.

title: What Makes a Great PCB Design Review Submission?
